about: Special relativity for TU Wien's Relativitätstheorie course of summer 2017, which left no script and no exercises: the labs follow Einstein (1905), Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper, by section and printed page, checked against the scanned original on 1 Nov 2026 (AUDIT.md). Notation is modern; each equation's note names Einstein's symbols. The low-speed field transformation is cross-checked with Prechtl (2010), Vorlesungen über Elektrodynamik, eq. (2.43); the point-charge potential with its eq. (3.13), p. 61, whose negative gradient is Coulomb's field. Free fall follows Einstein (1916), Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie, §§ 2, 21–22, checked against the scan on 8 Nov 2026. Maxwell's equations themselves are in the Electrodynamics Lab. Practice answers are worked by hand; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

lectures.title: Kinematic part: two frames, moving clocks and rods, adding velocities
Electrodynamic part: the Maxwell–Hertz equations in a moving frame
Gravitation: the falling frame and the Newtonian limit

labs.title: Minkowski diagram
labs.idea: Each frame has its own now. A moving frame's time and space axes tilt towards the light cone, and the two frames disagree on which events are simultaneous, yet agree on the interval.
labs.law: t' = γ (t − v x/c0²)    x' = γ (x − v t)    γ = 1/√(1 − (v/c0)²)

equations.eq: t' = γ (t − v x/c0²),  x' = γ (x − v t),  y' = y,  z' = z
equations.tex: t' = \gamma \Big(t - \frac{v}{c_0^2}\, x\Big), \qquad x' = \gamma (x - v t), \qquad y' = y, \qquad z' = z
equations.note: the Lorentz transformation from K to k moving at v along x; Einstein writes τ, ξ, η, ζ for t', x', y', z', β for γ and V for c0
Einstein's β, with V for c0

equations.eq: x² + y² + z² = c0² t²  ⇒  x'² + y'² + z'² = c0² t'²
equations.note: a light sphere stays a light sphere; Einstein: ξ² + η² + ζ² = V² τ²
the interval, for any event; Einstein shows it only for the light sphere

practice.question: A frame moves at 0.6 c0. What is its Lorentz factor γ?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 902; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Moving clocks and rods
labs.idea: A clock moving past you runs slow and a rod moving along its length is short, both by the same factor √(1 − (v/c0)²).

equations.note: axes of a moving sphere of radius R, seen from K (Einstein: V for c0)
reading τ of a clock resting in k, at x = v t; Einstein's own symbol τ
the moving clock's lag, up to terms of fourth and higher order

practice.question: A clock moves at 0.8 c0. How much time does it show while 10 s pass in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 904; the course left no exercise collection

practice.question: A 1 m rod moves along its length at 0.6 c0. How long is it, measured in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 903; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Adding velocities
labs.idea: Speeds do not simply add: two speeds below c always give one below c, and light keeps c in every frame.

equations.note: motion of a point moving at (w_x', w_y') in k, seen from K; Einstein writes w_ξ, w_η

equations.eq: U = √((v² + w² + 2 v w cos α) − (v w sin α/c0)²)/(1 + v w cos α/c0²)
equations.tex: U = \frac{\sqrt{(v^2 + w^2 + 2 v w \cos\alpha) - (v w \sin\alpha / c_0)^2}}{1 + v w \cos\alpha / c_0^2}
equations.note: resulting speed, α the angle between v and w
both along x
light composed with any slower speed

practice.question: A ship flies at 0.5 c0 and fires a probe forward at 0.5 c0 relative to itself. How fast is the probe in the resting frame?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 906; the course left no exercise collection

labs.title: Fields of a moving charge
labs.idea: Electric and magnetic fields are one field seen from different frames: a charge at rest has only E, the same charge moving has a flattened E and a B.
labs.law: E'_y = γ (E_y − v B_z)    E'_z = γ (E_z + v B_y)    B'_y = γ (B_y + v E_z/c0²)    B'_z = γ (B_z − v E_y/c0²)

equations.eq: E'_x = E_x,  E'_y = γ (E_y − (v/c0) B_z),  E'_z = γ (E_z + (v/c0) B_y)
equations.tex: E'_x = E_x, \qquad E'_y = \gamma \Big(E_y - \frac{v}{c_0} B_z\Big), \qquad E'_z = \gamma \Big(E_z + \frac{v}{c_0} B_y\Big)
equations.note: electric force in k, in the paper's Gaussian units; Einstein writes X, Y, Z for E and L, M, N for B

equations.eq: B'_x = B_x,  B'_y = γ (B_y + (v/c0) E_z),  B'_z = γ (B_z − (v/c0) E_y)
equations.tex: B'_x = B_x, \qquad B'_y = \gamma \Big(B_y + \frac{v}{c_0} E_z\Big), \qquad B'_z = \gamma \Big(B_z - \frac{v}{c_0} E_y\Big)
equations.note: magnetic force in k, Gaussian units (Einstein's L', M', N')

equations.eq: E'_x = E_x,  E'_y = γ (E_y − v B_z),  E'_z = γ (E_z + v B_y)
equations.tex: E'_x = E_x, \qquad E'_y = \gamma (E_y - v B_z), \qquad E'_z = \gamma (E_z + v B_y)
equations.note: the same in SI: the Gaussian B becomes c0 B, a common unit factor cancels

equations.eq: B'_x = B_x,  B'_y = γ (B_y + v E_z/c0²),  B'_z = γ (B_z − v E_y/c0²)
equations.tex: B'_x = B_x, \qquad B'_y = \gamma \Big(B_y + \frac{v}{c_0^2} E_z\Big), \qquad B'_z = \gamma \Big(B_z - \frac{v}{c_0^2} E_y\Big)
equations.note: in SI

equations.eq: E' = E + v × B,  B' = B
equations.note: the low-speed form, |v| ≪ c0, in Prechtl (2010), p. 38

equations.eq: E = Q γ r/(4πε0 (γ² x² + y² + z²)^{3/2}),  B = v × E/c0²
equations.note: a charge passing the origin at v, at that moment: Coulomb's field from the potential of Prechtl (2010) (3.13), p. 61, carried over with p. 909

practice.question: A frame moves at 10⁶ m/s across a pure magnetic field of 1 T. What electric field strength does it see?
practice.solution: E'_y = γ (0 − v B_z) with γ = 1.0000056, so |E'| = 1.000 × 10⁶ V/m; Prechtl's v × B gives the same to 5 digits (they differ by 5.6 parts per million).
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1905), p. 909; the course left no exercise collection

labs.lawTex: E'_y = \gamma (E_y - v B_z), \qquad E'_z = \gamma (E_z + v B_y), \qquad B'_y = \gamma \Big(B_y + \frac{v}{c_0^2} E_z\Big), \qquad B'_z = \gamma \Big(B_z - \frac{v}{c_0^2} E_y\Big)

labs.title: Free fall and the falling frame
labs.idea: Gravity is not a force you feel in free fall: in a frame falling with a thrown ball, the ball moves in a straight line. Seen from the ground the same line, and the grid with it, bends into an arch.
labs.law: x = x_fall − g t²/2    d²x/dt² = −½ c0² ∂g44/∂x

equations.note: height on the ground of a point at x_fall in a frame falling from rest; Einstein's frame K' accelerated against K is equivalent to a field (pp. 772–773)
the geodesic of slow motion in a weak static field: g44/2 plays the Newtonian potential, and only g44 enters; Einstein's units, c = 1
a uniform field in SI, from (67) with the potential g x
coordinate time per tick of a clock at rest: the clock runs slower near masses

equations.eq: x = v t − g t²/2,  x_max = v²/(2g),  t_flight = 2v/g
equations.tex: x = v t - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2, \qquad x_{\max} = \frac{v^2}{2g}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{flight}} = \frac{2v}{g}
equations.note: the thrown ball, the straight line x_fall = v t carried to the ground

practice.question: A ball is thrown straight up at 10 m/s where g = 9.81 m/s². How high does it rise?
practice.source: Worked by hand from the falling-frame line of Einstein (1916), pp. 772–773; the course left no exercise collection

practice.question: A clock stands 1000 m above another in a field of 9.81 m/s². How much more does it show after one day (86 400 s)?
practice.source: Worked by hand from Einstein (1916), (72), p. 820; the course left no exercise collection

labs.lawTex: x = x_{\mathrm{fall}} - \tfrac{1}{2} g t^2, \qquad \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = -\frac{c_0^2}{2}\, \frac{\partial g_{44}}{\partial x}
